questions.question: Why is a layered architecture considered necessary for organizing network design despite the enormous complexity of modern networks?

options.A: It eliminates the need for any protocol standards.
options.B: It provides a structured way to discuss and manage system components.
options.C: It forces all devices to implement every layer equally.
options.D: It guarantees zero duplicate functionality across layers.

questions.explanation:
Layered architecture offers a structured way to discuss system components, helping to manage complexity (Page 47)【Page 47】.  

---

questions.question: Which of the following factors is most directly considered when designing the boundaries between network layers?

options.A: The physical distance between network devices.
options.B: The desire to achieve modularity and separation of concerns.
options.C: The brand of hardware used in routers.

questions.explanation:
Designers consider modularity and separation of concerns to allow easier updates and clearer responsibilities (Page 49)【Page 49】.  

---

questions.question: How does modularity, as provided by layering, specifically aid in updating system components?

options.A: By requiring all layers to be rewritten simultaneously.
options.B: By allowing changes in one layer without affecting others.
options.C: By making the physical hardware interchangeable.
options.D: By eliminating the need for encapsulation.

questions.explanation:
Modularity means a change in one layer can be made independently of others, simplifying updates (Page 49)【Page 49】.  

---

questions.question: Which potential drawback of layering reflects a violation of the goal of separating layers?

options.A: Providing error recovery at both link and end‑to‑end levels.
options.C: A layer needing information (e.g., a timestamp) that exists only in another layer.
options.D: Using encapsulation to add headers at each layer.

questions.explanation:
When a layer requires data from another layer, it breaches the separation principle (Page 49)【Page 49】.  

---

questions.question: Why might duplicate functionality across layers, such as error recovery at both link and end‑to‑end levels, be considered a drawback?

options.C: It can lead to unnecessary overhead and inefficiency.
options.D: It prevents routers from implementing higher layers.

questions.explanation:
Duplicate error recovery can cause extra overhead, reducing efficiency (Page 49)【Page 49】.  

---

questions.question: Hosts implement all five layers of the protocol stack, while routers typically implement only the bottom layers. What rationale best explains this difference?

options.A: Hosts need full functionality for end‑to‑end communication, whereas routers primarily forward packets.
options.B: Routers are prohibited by standards from using transport‑layer protocols.
options.C: Hosts lack the hardware to skip any layers.
options.D: Implementing all layers on routers would violate the Internet’s edge‑centric design.

questions.explanation:
Hosts require complete end‑to‑end services, while routers focus on forwarding, thus implementing only layers 1‑3 (Page 53)【Page 53】.  

---

questions.question: In the encapsulation process, what situation can cause a large message to be divided into multiple transport‑layer segments and subsequently multiple network‑layer datagrams?

options.A: When the message size exceeds the maximum transmission unit (MTU) of the underlying link.
options.B: When the sender wants to increase security by fragmenting data.
options.C: When the receiver requests a specific number of segments.
options.D: When the application layer decides the segment size arbitrarily.

questions.explanation:
A large message may be split into segments and datagrams if it exceeds the link’s MTU, leading to multiple encapsulation steps (Page 54)【Page 54】.  

---

questions.question: Evaluate the statement: “Layering provides a structured way to discuss system components, which is an advantage for network designers.” Which of the following best supports this evaluation?

options.A: It forces every device to adopt the same hardware specifications.
options.B: It allows designers to reason about each layer’s responsibilities independently.
options.C: It eliminates the need for protocol standards across the Internet.
options.D: It ensures that no layer ever needs to interact with another.

questions.explanation:
Structured discussion enables designers to focus on individual layer responsibilities (Page 49)【Page 49】.  

---

questions.question: Considering the potential drawback of duplicate error recovery, how should a network designer evaluate the trade‑off between link‑layer and end‑to‑end error handling?

options.A: Always disable link‑layer error recovery to rely solely on end‑to‑end mechanisms.
options.B: Prefer link‑layer recovery for local errors and end‑to‑end recovery for end‑to‑end reliability.
options.C: Implement both mechanisms identically to maximize redundancy.
options.D: Remove all error recovery to simplify the protocol stack.

questions.explanation:
A balanced approach uses link‑layer recovery for local issues and end‑to‑end recovery for overall reliability, mitigating duplication concerns (Page 49)【Page 49】.  

---

questions.question: When might a designer deliberately allow a layer to access information from another layer, despite the principle of separation?

options.A: When the lower layer’s timestamp is required for accurate end‑to‑end latency measurement.
options.B: When the upper layer wishes to modify physical cable lengths.
options.C: When the design aims to eliminate all encapsulation.
options.D: When the network has exactly five layers.

questions.explanation: Accessing a lower‑layer timestamp can be justified for precise latency calculations, even though it breaches strict separation (Page 49)【Page 49】.
